headline: Claims Quillen's 1978 conjecture on subgroup posets for every finite group and every prime, in a stronger homology form.
scope: Every finite group and every prime, in the rational-homology form; the odd-prime case was already deduced by Díaz Ramos in 2026.
plain: For a finite group and a prime p, Quillen built a shape from its small p-subgroups. If the group has a nontrivial normal p-subgroup, this shape can be shrunk to a point. Quillen conjectured the converse in 1978. Earlier work settled odd primes and narrowed the prime two to a few families. This paper claims the remaining cases, with a stronger conclusion: the shape always has a hole visible to rational homology.
doesNot: This does not give a new proof of the odd-prime case from scratch; it uses earlier reductions and results for most cases.
origin: This result comes from an unreleased OpenAI model, published in the openai/math release on 6 October 2026.

scorecard.firstStepBy: Daniel Quillen, homotopy properties of the poset of nontrivial p-subgroups
scorecard.significanceWhy: It claims to finish a well-known 1978 conjecture in finite group theory after decades of partial reductions.

explanation:
Take the group S₃ of all reorderings of three objects, and the prime 2. An elementary abelian 2-subgroup is a subgroup where every element squares to the identity and any two commute. S₃ has three such subgroups besides the trivial one. Each is a single swap of two objects together with the identity. None contains another. So Quillen's shape for S₃ is three separate points. Three points cannot shrink to one point. Reduced homology counts this: it has rank 3 − 1 = 2.

Now take A₄, the even reorderings of four objects. It has three subgroups of order 2 and one of order 4 that contains all three. So the shape is a cone over the three points, which shrinks to a point. The difference is that A₄ has a normal 2-subgroup, the one of order 4. A normal subgroup is one that conjugation by any element maps to itself. A nontrivial normal p-subgroup always makes the shape contractible[3].

Quillen conjectured the converse in 1978. He proved it for solvable groups and some other families[4]. The almost-simple case came next[5]. Aschbacher and Smith then reduced the problem for primes above 5 to special cases of unitary groups. Díaz Ramos later deduced the rational-homology form for every finite group at odd primes[6]. At the prime two, successive steps narrowed the remaining families[7]. The obstacle was the last families of classical groups at the prime two.

This paper claims the conjecture for all finite groups and all primes[1]. It claims a stronger form. If the group has no nontrivial normal p-subgroup, the shape has nonzero rational homology[2]. Rational homology counts holes with rational-number coefficients. So the shape has a real hole, not just a failure to shrink. With the converse, a fixed field of coefficients detects exactly when such a normal subgroup exists[8].

To build the needed holes, the paper uses frames. A frame splits a vector space into lines[9]. Flipping signs on each line gives an elementary abelian subgroup. The paper links frames that differ only inside a plane, so that boundary terms cancel[10]. This produces cycles, which are the holes it needs.

How sure is this? There is no Lean check. A computer proof checker has not looked at any part of it. The proof depends on several earlier reductions and on case-by-case work for families of groups. No specialist review of the paper has been published.
hypeCheck: Major if the proof holds. Much of the reduction was done in earlier work. There is no Lean check and no published specialist review.

glossary.meaning: A subgroup where any two elements commute and every element raised to the power p gives the identity.
The shape built from the nontrivial elementary abelian p-subgroups, with a link for each inclusion.
A subgroup that conjugation by any element of the group maps to itself.
Able to be shrunk continuously to a single point.
An algebraic count of holes, adjusted so that a single point counts as zero.
A splitting of a vector space into lines.
